tagline: West Africa's Atlantic gateway, its islands still reached by open chaloupe
summary: Dakar occupies the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of continental Africa, wrapping a sheltered eastern harbour that has been the region's dominant port for a century. The city's marine identity is anchored by Gorede Island — a UNESCO World Heritage site and slave-trade memorial two-and-a-half nautical miles offshore — reached today only by a public chaloupe from the downtown terminal. North of the peninsula, Ngor Island, the fishing village of Yoff, and the Iles de la Madeleine national park sit minutes offshore but are served by informal pirogues. The bay is calm and swell-protected on its eastern flank, and Dakar already sustains dense app-based ride-hail demand, making it a natural node for scheduled and on-demand water links that today have no reliable, weatherproof operator.

use_cases.title: Heritage island shuttle
use_cases.body: A scheduled, weatherproof link from the downtown terminal to Gorede replaces the single ageing chaloupe, adding sailings at peak and removing the daily bottleneck for heritage tourism.

use_cases.title: Northern island day-hopper
use_cases.body: On-demand runs to Ngor Island and the Iles de la Madeleine national park give visitors a safe, insured alternative to informal pirogues.

use_cases.title: Bay commuter bypass
use_cases.body: A waterborne link along the sheltered eastern bay lets commuters skip the congested corniche into the business district.

use_cases.title: Airport-coast connector
use_cases.body: Blaise Diagne International sits inland at Diass; a coastal water leg can feed peninsula hotels and the northern beaches from a shuttle point.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Ideal for the 2–5 nm island and bay hops — Gorede, Ngor, Madeleine — where calm eastern-bay water and short legs favour a fast, quiet, zero-wake craft that can hold a reliable timetable the chaloupe cannot.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Reserved for longer coastal runs toward the Petite Cote (Saly, Mbour) and Saloum delta approaches, where range matters more than turn frequency.

transit_planning: Senegal's transport modernisation has focused on the BRT and the Dakar-Diamniadio regional express rail; the waterfront remains served by a single legacy Gorede chaloupe and informal pirogues. A structured marine layer complements the land network by unlocking the island and bay corridors that road and rail cannot reach.

competitive_landscape: The Dakar-Gorede link is a public monopoly run with a single ageing chaloupe on a fixed timetable; the northern islands are served only by informal pirogues with no insurance, schedule or safety oversight. There is no on-demand, weatherproof operator on the peninsula. Land-side, ride-hail apps are mature and dense, but no player bridges the water — leaving the island and bay corridors structurally underserved.
seasonality: The Atlantic swell and harmattan wind pick up December–March, occasionally disrupting the exposed northern-island pirogue runs; the sheltered eastern bay toward Gorede stays workable year-round. The dry season (November–May) is peak tourism; the July–October rains soften demand but keep the bay calm.
regulatory_note: Senegal's maritime affairs fall under the Agence Nationale des Affaires Maritimes; passenger craft on the Gorede run are already licensed and inspected, so a modern operator slots into an existing permitting frame rather than creating one. Heritage-site access at Gorede is coordinated with the culture ministry, and any added sailings would be scheduled with the existing terminal authority.

precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates durable, year-round island passenger demand that a single legacy craft cannot fully serve.
Shows the user base is already comfortable summoning mobility on an app — the behavioural bridge to on-demand water transport.
